entries.title: Benny's Video
entries.what: Haneke's Austrian drama: a teenager who watches everything through a camcorder kills a girl he has just met, and his parents set about managing the consequences
entries.why: The second film of the trilogy Haneke himself groups The Seventh Continent into, made by the same director in the same clinical register and about the same middle-class emotional deadness; the killing happens in a fixed frame at the edge of the image, and the parents' response is logistics, not grief

entries.title: 71 Fragments of a Chronology of Chance
entries.what: Haneke assembles seventy-one unconnected scraps of Viennese life that end when a student shoots strangers in a bank queue and then himself
entries.why: The third and closing part of the trilogy Haneke says The Seventh Continent begins; it takes the earlier film's method to its limit, building the whole picture out of numbered fragments of routine with black leader between them and refusing any causal account of the massacre

entries.title: Funny Games
entries.what: Two polite young men take a holidaying Austrian family hostage at their lake house and torture them to death over a night, addressing the audience as they go
entries.why: Same director, same target: a bourgeois family unit dismantled with method rather than passion. The violence stays offscreen and the aftermath stays onscreen, which is exactly the inversion The Seventh Continent performs on the money down the toilet and the fish on the carpet

entries.title: Code Unknown
entries.what: Haneke's Parisian mosaic: a crumpled pastry bag tossed into a Romanian beggar's lap on a boulevard detonates through the lives of an actress, an African drumming teacher, the beggar and a war photographer, in unbroken real-time takes separated by black
entries.why: The formal sibling of The Seventh Continent — a film built entirely of discrete blocks with the connective tissue cut out, each block ending before it resolves. Its own subtitle, 'Incomplete Tales of Several Journeys', describes the earlier film's method applied to a city instead of a household

entries.title: Caché
entries.what: A Parisian television intellectual and his wife receive anonymous videotapes of their own front door, and the tapes lead back to a childhood betrayal he will not admit to
entries.why: Haneke's most exact study of what a comfortable family does when its surface is punctured: the frames are locked off, the crucial act arrives without warning in a single unbroken shot, and the film ends refusing to tell you who sent the tapes. The same withholding of motive that makes The Seventh Continent unbearable

entries.title: The Piano Teacher
entries.what: A Vienna conservatory professor living with her mother pursues a masochistic contract with a student, and self-harm is filmed as household procedure
entries.why: Haneke again, and the closest he comes to The Seventh Continent's specific subject: a person methodically destroying herself inside an apartment, with the camera flat and unhelpful and the mutilation treated as one more domestic task. Shot in the same Viennese petit-bourgeois interiors

entries.title: Amour
entries.what: Two retired Parisian music teachers stay in their apartment after the wife's stroke, until the husband ends her life and seals the room
entries.why: The Seventh Continent's structure turned late and tender: a couple decide, inside one flat, to bring their life to an ordered close, and the film gives you the routine of it — meals, washing, the piano, the flowers — with no score and no scene of decision. The apartment is again the whole world, and again it is shut up at the end

entries.title: Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles
entries.what: Chantal Akerman films three days of a Brussels widow's housework, cooking and afternoon prostitution in real time and fixed frames, ending in a sudden killing
entries.why: The anchor of the whole tradition The Seventh Continent works in: domestic routine given so much screen time, at eye level and without commentary, that the routine itself becomes the horror, and violence arrives as one more gesture in the sequence rather than as a climax. If a viewer took one thing from Haneke's film it is this texture

entries.title: L'Argent
entries.what: Bresson's last film: a forged banknote passed as a prank ruins an honest delivery man, who ends by murdering a farm family with an axe
entries.why: Bresson is the filmmaker Haneke names first among his own, and this is the film of his that The Seventh Continent most resembles — money handled as an object, actions shown as hands and surfaces, the annihilation of a household delivered with no music, no motive speech and no reaction shot. Haneke's toilet-flushing sequence is Bressonian montage applied to banknotes

entries.title: The Devil, Probably
entries.what: A Parisian student, disgusted by ecology, politics and analysis alike, arranges for someone else to shoot him in Père-Lachaise
entries.why: Bresson, whom Haneke names as a favourite filmmaker, on the precise subject: a planned suicide by a person with no diagnosable grievance, presented flatly and without the film supplying a reason. The Seventh Continent's refusal to explain why a solvent, employed family kills itself is this film's argument carried into a nuclear household

entries.title: Why Does Herr R. Run Amok?
entries.what: Fassbinder and Michael Fengler follow a mild West German draughtsman through long takes of office chat and family evenings until he beats his wife, son and neighbour to death and hangs himself at work
entries.why: The direct precursor, down to the question in the title being refused an answer. Everything before the killing is banal small talk held in unbroken takes; the murders happen in one flat shot with no score; the film ends on an announcement rather than a reckoning. The Seventh Continent is this film's method applied to a family that kills itself rather than one man who kills his

entries.title: Dog Days
entries.what: Ulrich Seidl's first fiction feature: a heatwave in a Viennese commuter suburb of identical bungalows, six storylines of humiliation, sex and low-grade cruelty among people with nothing to say to each other
entries.why: The central document of the Austrian clinical strain The Seventh Continent founded, and a direct crew relative — Markus Schleinzer cast both this and Haneke's Piano Teacher in 2001. Seidl's frontal, symmetrical tableaux of consumer interiors, non-actors held past comfort and violence that arrives without build-up are Haneke's grammar pushed further towards the documentary

entries.title: Michael
entries.what: Markus Schleinzer's debut: the orderly domestic life of an Austrian insurance company employee who keeps a ten-year-old boy in a soundproofed cellar, filmed as household routine
entries.why: Made by Haneke's own casting director — Schleinzer cast The Piano Teacher, Time of the Wolf and The White Ribbon — and it is the purest inheritance of The Seventh Continent's method: the abuse is entirely offscreen, the film gives you the dishes, the Christmas tree and the ski trip instead, and it withholds every explanatory interior

entries.title: Safe
entries.what: Todd Haynes films a San Fernando Valley housewife who becomes allergic to her own surroundings — furniture, perfume, freeway air — and retreats to a desert wellness compound
entries.why: The American film that shares The Seventh Continent's actual thesis: consumer domestic space as something that quietly poisons the people inside it. Haynes holds Carol in wide, static frames that dwarf her, lets the sofa and the new couch carry the scenes, gives no diagnosis and no recovery, and ends on a refusal of comfort as complete as Haneke's

entries.title: The White Ribbon
entries.what: Haneke's black-and-white account of a north German village before the First World War where children are disciplined into piety and a series of cruelties goes unsolved
entries.why: Same director, same method of withholding: the crimes are never attributed, the camera stays fixed and frontal, there is no score, and the film ends by refusing to close. Graded 2 rather than 3 only because the period setting removes the consumer-present that The Seventh Continent is specifically about

entries.title: Time of the Wolf
entries.what: After an unnamed catastrophe a bourgeois family drives to their country house, the father is shot in the first minutes, and the mother and children join a crowd waiting at a railway siding for a train that may not come
entries.why: Haneke again, and the flipside of The Seventh Continent: the same middle-class family unit stripped of its objects, this time by the world rather than by its own decision. Extended scenes in near-total darkness, no explanation of the disaster, no rescue

entries.title: Funny Games
entries.what: Haneke's shot-for-shot English-language remake of his own 1997 film, with an American family at the lake house
entries.why: The same director restaging the same annihilation of a family in the same frames, which makes it a legitimate recommendation; graded 2 rather than 3 because it adds nothing to the original's argument and a viewer sent here instead of to the 1997 film has been slightly short-changed

entries.title: Happy End
entries.what: A wealthy Calais construction family manages a site accident, a grandfather who wants to die and a teenage girl who has quietly poisoned her own mother and films the family on her phone
entries.why: Haneke's late return to this material: the poisoning is captured on a phone in vertical video and read by everyone as a suicide attempt, the grandfather shops for a way out, and no one in the house responds to any of it. Same bourgeois death drive, same offscreen violence, same screens standing in for family life — but a more dispersed, more satirical film that dilutes the earlier one's concentration

entries.title: Mouchette
entries.what: Bresson follows a humiliated village girl through her last day, ending as she rolls herself down a bank into a pond
entries.why: Bresson, named by Haneke among his favourite filmmakers, on a suicide filmed as a physical procedure with no interior access and no lament. The final gesture is repeated until it works, the way The Seventh Continent repeats the smashing until the room is gone

entries.title: Au hasard Balthazar
entries.what: The life of a donkey passed between owners in rural France, each of whom uses it up, intercut with the parallel ruin of the girl who first loved it
entries.why: The Bresson film Haneke has repeatedly named as the one he values most, and the source of the technique The Seventh Continent runs on: people reduced to hands and objects, emotion withheld from the performances entirely, meaning assembled by cutting rather than stated

entries.title: Une femme douce
entries.what: Bresson opens with a woman going off a Paris balcony and spends the film on her pawnbroker husband's flat, unreliable account of the marriage that preceded it
entries.why: A suicide inside a bourgeois marriage, told from the objects outward — the table, the shawl on the balcony, the possessions counted up — by the filmmaker Haneke names first. Its coldness towards a death it has already shown you is the register The Seventh Continent works in for two hours

entries.title: L'Eclisse
entries.what: Antonioni's Rome: a woman leaves one man, half-begins with a stockbroker, and the film ends with seven minutes of the street corner where they agreed to meet, without either of them
entries.why: Antonioni is named among Haneke's favourite filmmakers, and critics read Haneke's held shots as Antonioni's temps mort — the shot that continues after the story has stopped. The closing montage of empty objects and lit lamps is the direct ancestor of The Seventh Continent's inventory of a life reduced to surfaces

entries.title: Germany, Year Zero
entries.what: Rossellini follows a twelve-year-old scavenging in the ruins of Berlin, who poisons his invalid father on a scrap of Nazi advice and then walks off a bombed-out building
entries.why: Rossellini is on Haneke's list of favourite filmmakers, and this is the great precedent for a domestic killing and a suicide filmed without music, without a confession scene and without the film breaking stride. Grade and tone diverge: the neorealist street photography, the location bustle and the scored pathos are a warmer surface than Haneke's locked-off interiors

entries.title: Import/Export
entries.what: Seidl crosses two journeys: a Ukrainian nurse going west into an Austrian geriatric ward, and a Viennese security guard going east to install slot machines
entries.why: The Austrian clinical strain at its most rigorous — frontal static tableaux, non-professionals held far past comfort, no score, degradation filmed as ordinary procedure. The geriatric ward scenes do to institutional routine what The Seventh Continent does to a breakfast table

entries.title: Lovely Rita
entries.what: Jessica Hausner's debut: an apathetic Austrian schoolgirl drifts through small rebellions in a suburban Catholic household, then takes the revolver from her father's basement shooting range and kills both her parents before getting on a train
entries.why: Austrian family annihilation in Haneke's exact register, and a crew relative — Markus Schleinzer cast this in the same year he cast The Piano Teacher. Hausner shoots the parents' house as a set of flat, symmetrical rooms, gives Rita no stated motive, cuts away before each shooting and simply stops

entries.title: Hotel
entries.what: Hausner's second feature: a new receptionist at an Alpine hotel asks what happened to the woman whose job she took, and the film declines to say
entries.why: Cast by Schleinzer, Haneke's casting director, and built on the same principle of the withheld cause: rigid symmetrical frames of corridors and staff rooms, a dread with no supplied source, and an ending that removes a person without an account of it

entries.title: Lourdes
entries.what: Hausner's account of an organised pilgrimage: a wheelchair-using woman with MS goes through the baths, the processions and the group meals, and appears to be cured
entries.why: The purest Austrian application of the static frame to institutional routine — the rosary, the trays, the queue for the grotto, all in locked-off symmetrical shots with no score. It refuses to say whether the miracle is real exactly as The Seventh Continent refuses to say why the family decides

entries.title: Revanche
entries.what: Götz Spielmann's Austrian thriller: a Vienna brothel worker and her ex-convict lover attempt a bank robbery, she is shot dead, and he ends up chopping wood on a farm next door to the policeman who fired
entries.why: Austria's other clinical filmmaker, working in long static takes without a note of score, and shooting a killing as an accident with no dramatic punctuation at all. The long silent stretches of farm labour take the Haneke routine block and use it to hold grief offscreen

entries.title: Goodnight Mommy
entries.what: Veronika Franz and Severin Fiala's Austrian film: twin boys in a modernist lakeside house decide the bandaged woman who came back from surgery is not their mother, and tie her up
entries.why: Austrian family horror from inside Seidl's circle — Franz is his longtime co-writer — built on the same antiseptic design-magazine interior and the same withholding of what is actually going on. Grade and tone diverge: it escalates into onscreen torture and a genre reveal, which is louder and more explanatory than anything Haneke permits

entries.title: Angst
entries.what: Gerald Kargl's Austrian film, built on the real case of Werner Kniesek: a man released from prison walks into a suburban villa and murders the family inside over an afternoon
entries.why: The Austrian family-annihilation film that precedes Haneke, from the same country and the same suburban milieu, and a real reference point for what The Seventh Continent's audience was already carrying. Grade and tone diverge hard: Kargl gives you a continuous explanatory voiceover, a Klaus Schulze synth score and a famously restless overhead camera — everything Haneke strips out. Worth knowing as the opposite solution to the same subject

entries.title: Longing
entries.what: Valeska Grisebach films a village metalworker and volunteer fireman, happily married, who begins an affair after a conference and attempts to shoot himself
entries.why: The Berlin School at its most affectless: non-professionals from the village playing themselves, no score, scenes that end before their point is made, and a suicide attempt whose motive the film explicitly declines to supply. The closing device — the story retold secondhand by children — refuses catharsis in the same way Haneke's title card does

entries.title: Time Out
entries.what: Laurent Cantet's film, loosely drawn from the Jean-Claude Romand case: a French consultant who has been sacked spends months driving between motorway service stations, inventing a job in Geneva and taking money from friends
entries.why: The nearest thing in French cinema to The Seventh Continent's subject — a middle-class man dismantling his own life by increments while the routine holds — filmed in cold blue glass-and-car-park exteriors with long quiet takes and no crisis scene. Cantet withholds the Romand case's family murders, which sharpens rather than softens the dread

entries.title: La Cérémonie
entries.what: Chabrol's film of a Ruth Rendell novel: an illiterate housekeeper and a postmistress befriend each other and shoot a cultured provincial family dead in their drawing room during a televised opera
entries.why: A bourgeois family destroyed in its own house by people it barely sees, with the massacre staged as an almost administrative act and the class reading left entirely to the viewer. Isabelle Huppert links it directly to Haneke, who cast her twice. Grade and tone diverge: Chabrol's glossy surfaces, score and novelistic plotting are a warmer, more readable register than Haneke's

entries.title: Dogtooth
entries.what: Yorgos Lanthimos's Greek film: a father keeps his three adult children inside the family compound with an invented vocabulary and invented dangers beyond the fence
entries.why: The family as a closed system engineered by its parents until it destroys itself from within, shot in flat, frontal, often decapitating frames with no score, violence delivered deadpan and no explanation of how the arrangement began. The clearest descendant of Haneke outside the German-speaking world

entries.title: Elephant
entries.what: Gus Van Sant tracks students through a suburban American high school on an ordinary morning, looping the same minutes from several points of view, until two boys begin shooting
entries.why: A massacre presented as a sequence of corridors, lunch trays and photography club — routine given the running time, motive explicitly refused, the killing itself made banal and the film ending mid-act with no reckoning. It is 71 Fragments' argument in a different country, and shares The Seventh Continent's conviction that explanation would be a lie

entries.title: Last Days
entries.what: Van Sant's fictionalised final days of a Kurt Cobain figure, wandering a damp estate, mumbling, cooking, avoiding people, until his body is found in the greenhouse
entries.why: A suicide filmed entirely as unremarkable behaviour: the film gives you the macaroni, the shotgun catalogue, the doorbell, and gives you no interior monologue, no build and no aftermath. The withheld motive and the long unhelpful takes put it squarely in The Seventh Continent's register

entries.title: Taste of Cherry
entries.what: Kiarostami's Iranian film: a man drives the dirt roads above Tehran looking for someone willing to bury him after he takes pills in a hole he has already dug
entries.why: A planned suicide by a man whose reasons the film never states — the question is raised several times and refused — presented as a series of flat, repetitive car journeys with no score. The methodical preparation of one's own death as the entire plot is precisely The Seventh Continent's spine

entries.title: The Headless Woman
entries.what: Lucrecia Martel's Argentine film: a bourgeois dentist hits something on a country road, drives on, and her extended family quietly erases the evidence that anything occurred
entries.why: The decisive act happens offscreen and stays there, the class machinery of denial is shown rather than explained, and the frames are cluttered, off-centre and deliberately unhelpful about where to look. A film about a comfortable family managing an atrocity by not naming it, which is the manner The Seventh Continent's parents apply to their own children

entries.title: Le Feu follet
entries.what: Louis Malle follows a recovering alcoholic through two days of visits to old Parisian friends before he shoots himself on the date he had set
entries.why: The template for a suicide film organised as a countdown of ordinary errands, with the decision made before the film starts and never argued about. Grade and tone diverge: Malle's Satie piano, the confessional dialogue and Ronet's expressive performance explain and mourn in a way Haneke's frames categorically will not

entries.title: Red Desert
entries.what: Antonioni's first colour film: an industrialist's wife drifts through the painted fog and chemical plants of Ravenna, unable to attach to her husband, her child or her lover
entries.why: Antonioni, whom Haneke names among his favourites, on the machine-made environment outpacing the people in it — the standard critical framing of what The Seventh Continent does to a consumer household. Graded 1 because the connection is thematic ancestry rather than method; tone 1 because Antonioni's expressive colour design and score are a far more authored surface than Haneke's flat interiors

entries.title: La Notte
entries.what: Antonioni gives a Milanese novelist and his wife one day and one industrialist's party across which their marriage silently finishes
entries.why: A marriage ending without an argument, in a modern city that has nothing to offer either of them — the anomie lineage Haneke is routinely placed in. Graded 1: the kinship is ancestral, and the film's elegant movement, jazz and star performances are a more legible pleasure than The Seventh Continent offers

entries.title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
entries.what: Pasolini transposes Sade to the Republic of Salò: four fascist dignitaries take a group of teenagers to a villa and work through a catalogue of degradation
entries.why: Pasolini is on Haneke's list of favourite filmmakers, and this is the film usually cited when Haneke is discussed as a director who implicates the viewer in atrocity rather than staging it for pleasure. Graded 1 because the family subject is absent; tone 1 because the film's structure is explicit, declamatory and literary where Haneke is mute

entries.title: Mirror
entries.what: Tarkovsky's autobiographical film assembles childhood, his mother, wartime newsreel and poetry into an associative rather than narrative whole
entries.why: Tarkovsky is among the filmmakers Haneke names as favourites, and the film is a formal precedent for a life told in unlabelled fragments rather than a plot. Grade and tone diverge as far as they can in this list: Tarkovsky's drifting camera, Bach, burning house and lyric memory are the opposite of the affect Haneke withholds. Included as an influence a model should know without being rewarded for the texture

entries.title: Lost Highway
entries.what: David Lynch's film: a jazz musician receives videotapes of the inside of his own house, is convicted of killing his wife, and becomes someone else in his cell
entries.why: Cited by critics — Serge Kaganski among them — as the model for Caché's opening surveillance tape, so a documented point of contact with Haneke's use of the anonymous video of a front door. Grade and tone diverge sharply: the industrial score, the dream logic and the expressionist lighting are a register Haneke has no interest in

entries.title: Je, tu, il, elle
entries.what: Akerman's first feature: a young woman alone in an emptied room eating sugar from a paper bag and rearranging furniture, then hitchhiking, then a night with a former lover
entries.why: Grade and tone diverge upward on tone: the connection to a family's collective suicide is thin, but the first third — a person in a bare room performing pointless domestic operations in long static takes with no music and no explanation — is as close to The Seventh Continent's texture as anything filmed

entries.title: Yella
entries.what: Christian Petzold's film: a woman leaves a failing east German town and her violent ex-husband for a venture capital job in Hanover, and the money talk begins to feel unreal
entries.why: The Berlin School's central figure on capital, precarity and people flattened by economic surfaces — the milieu The Seventh Continent's engineer and optometrist occupy. Graded 1 and tone 1: Petzold's sound design, ghost-story turn and closing reveal supply exactly the explanatory frame Haneke refuses

entries.title: The Forest for the Trees
entries.what: Maren Ade's debut: an eager young teacher moves to a new town, fails with her class and her one attempt at a friendship, and drives away
entries.why: German, affectless, and organised around social humiliation accumulating through unremarkable scenes until the protagonist simply exits. The abrupt, unexplained ending is a real formal echo. Graded 1: the handheld video texture, the comic cringe and the close observation of one performance sit at a distance from Haneke's locked frames

entries.title: Marseille
entries.what: Angela Schanelec's film: a Berlin photographer swaps flats with a woman in Marseille, comes home, and something is elided that the film never returns to
entries.why: Tone runs well ahead of grade here. The connection to a family suicide is remote, but Schanelec is the most rigorous of the Berlin School — fixed frames, flat non-performance, no score, whole events removed from between the scenes — and a viewer who admired The Seventh Continent's fragments will recognise the method exactly

entries.title: The Adversary
entries.what: Nicole Garcia's film of the Jean-Claude Romand case: a man who was never a doctor sustains the lie for eighteen years and then kills his wife, children and parents
entries.why: The literal subject — a middle-class French household annihilated by the father after a long, orderly deception — makes it an obvious neighbour. Graded and toned 1: Garcia builds it as a psychological case study with flashbacks, a score and a performance designed to let you in, which is the explanatory apparatus Haneke removes

entries.title: La Ciénaga
entries.what: Lucrecia Martel's debut: two related Argentine families rot through a summer around a filthy pool and a dark country house, ending with a child's fall from a ladder
entries.why: A family decomposing through inertia rather than event, with the catastrophe offscreen and unmourned in the final seconds. Graded 1 as an oblique relative; tone 1 because Martel's dense overlapping sound, roaming camera and bodily closeness are a sensuous register rather than Haneke's clinical one

entries.title: 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days
entries.what: Cristian Mungiu's film: two students arrange an illegal abortion in a Ceaușescu-era hotel room, and afterwards go to a family birthday dinner
entries.why: Tone outruns grade. The subject is not Haneke's, but the method is: unbroken static takes, no score, the worst moments held in one shot, the dinner-table scene playing in a single unmoving frame while the protagonist waits, and a final cut that denies resolution

entries.title: Vive L'Amour
entries.what: Tsai Ming-liang's film: three strangers in Taipei separately use an empty apartment for sale, barely speaking, ending in a park with a long unbroken take of a woman crying
entries.why: Near-wordless urban anomie built from routine — keys, water, a melon, a suicide attempt handled with no more emphasis than a meal — in very long static takes with no music at all. The connection to a family's self-destruction is loose, so grade 1, but the texture is a close match

entries.title: The Turin Horse
entries.what: Béla Tarr's last film: a carter and his daughter repeat the same six days of wind, boiled potatoes and drawing water until the well dries and the lamp will not light
entries.why: Routine filmed until routine is the whole content, then withdrawn — the closest thing in cinema to The Seventh Continent's structural argument, carried out over thirty shots. Graded 1 because the milieu could not be further from a Linz apartment; tone 2 without hesitation, allowing for Mihály Víg's continuous score, which is the one element Haneke would never permit

entries.title: The Killing of a Sacred Deer
entries.what: Lanthimos's film: a cardiac surgeon is told by a teenage boy that his wife and children will sicken and die unless he kills one of them himself
entries.why: A comfortable family that must destroy itself by decision, its members discussing the arithmetic flatly at the kitchen table. Graded 1 because the mechanism is supernatural rather than social; tone 1 because the blaring choral score, gliding steadicam and stylised line readings push it towards horror where Haneke stays mute

entries.title: Our Daily Bread
entries.what: Nikolaus Geyrhalter's Austrian documentary on industrial food production: hatcheries, abattoirs, greenhouses and salt mines, in immaculate symmetrical frames with no commentary
entries.why: Tone far ahead of grade. It is not about a family and has no story, but it is the Austrian clinical strain in its purest form — static wide frames, no narration, no score, industrial procedure shown at length and left entirely unjudged — and it is the natural companion piece to the supermarket and car-wash sequences in The Seventh Continent

entries.title: Force Majeure
entries.what: Ruben Östlund's film: a Swedish family on an Alpine skiing holiday comes apart after the father runs from an avalanche that turns out to be harmless
entries.why: A nuclear family dismantled over a few days in a designed hotel interior, filmed in long static wide shots that let the scenes go on past comfort. Graded and toned 1: Östlund's comedy, his Vivaldi stings and the explicit arguments in which the characters state the film's thesis are all things Haneke would cut

entries.title: We Need to Talk About Kevin
entries.what: Lynne Ramsay's film: a mother reconstructs her life with the son who murdered his father, his sister and his schoolmates with a bow
entries.why: The subject — family annihilation from inside a middle-class household, motive unavailable — is genuinely adjacent, so grade 1 is fair. Tone 0: Ramsay works in saturated red montage, fractured chronology, pop needle-drops and a mother's subjective anguish, which is an emotional machine of exactly the kind The Seventh Continent switches off. A model that offers this as a texture match has misread the target

entries.title: The Virgin Suicides
entries.what: Sofia Coppola's film: five sisters in 1970s suburban Michigan kill themselves, remembered years later by the neighbourhood boys who watched them
entries.why: A family's collective suicide with no supplied explanation, which is a real subject-level connection. Tone 0: gauzy light, Air's score, voiceover nostalgia and a romanticised mystery make the deaths beautiful, which is the single thing Haneke most refuses

entries.title: American Beauty
entries.what: Sam Mendes's film: a suburban advertising man quits his job, buys a sports car and lusts after his daughter's friend while his marriage and his neighbour's household collapse
entries.why: Everyone reaches for this when asked about consumerism and suburban emptiness, and the shared subject makes grade 1 defensible at most. Tone 0 is the point of including it: voiceover that explains every feeling, Thomas Newman's score, satire, uplift and a redemptive death. Recommending it for The Seventh Continent is the characteristic failure this list exists to catch

entries.title: Ordinary People
entries.what: Robert Redford's film: an affluent Illinois family cannot speak about the drowned older son, and the surviving boy, who attempted suicide, goes into therapy
entries.why: A middle-class family silently disintegrating around an unspoken death, and a suicide attempt in the house. Tone 0: the film's entire method is the talking cure — scenes exist so that feelings can be named aloud and released — which is the diametric opposite of a film that shows you a family destroying its furniture and tells you nothing

entries.title: You, the Living
entries.what: Roy Andersson's tableau film: some fifty static vignettes of Swedish people complaining, dreaming and failing to be understood, ending with bombers over the city
entries.why: The formal overlap is real but partial. Andersson shares the refusal to cut inside a scene and the reduction of a life to a series of drab boxed compositions. But The Seventh Continent's frames are mostly close, on hands, taps, banknotes and the toilet, and its withholding is clinical where Andersson's is comic; he is also finally affectionate about his people in a way Haneke never is. The companion suggestion, Songs from the Second Floor, is the stronger of the two.

entries.title: Songs from the Second Floor
entries.what: Roy Andersson's first feature in twenty-five years: fixed-camera tableaux of a European city in gridlock, including a man who has burned down his own furniture business and a child led up a cliff by economists
entries.why: Aims at the same target from another angle: Western European material comfort as a dead ritual its inhabitants perform without belief, filmed in fluorescent grey with the camera nailed down and nobody permitted to explain themselves. The climax is a human sacrifice carried out as an administrative decision, which is the exact horror The Seventh Continent produces when a family destroys everything it owns as a chore. Andersson's method is absurdist comedy and Haneke's is clinical realism; the surfaces and the coldness match regardless.

entries.title: The Hour of the Wolf
entries.what: Bergman's island film: a painter is consumed by insomnia and by demons who may be his neighbours, the whole recounted after the fact by his wife
entries.why: A married couple isolated to the point of annihilation, and one of the few art films that treats a private collapse as total. That is as far as the case runs, and it runs against the grain of the target. Bergman's film is wholly interior, told through dreams, flashbacks and a confession to camera, and its method is access to a mind; The Seventh Continent's power comes from refusing that access completely, offering no motive and no interiority at all. The suggestion recommends the opposite procedure on a related subject.

entries.title: Hunger
entries.what: Steve McQueen's debut: the 1981 Maze prison hunger strike given as physical procedure, the dirty protest and then Bobby Sands's starvation, with one seventeen-minute static conversation at the centre
entries.why: The closest film here to Haneke's method. A chosen self-destruction is shown as a sequence of tasks and bodily facts, in long fixed takes, with the camera as attentive to an orderly sweeping urine down a corridor as to a man dying, and with reaction shots and music withheld throughout. It sits naturally beside the key's Elephant and Last Days. What keeps it at grade 2 is meaning: Sands's act is public and argued, where Haneke's family act for no reason the film will ever supply.

entries.title: Woman in the Dunes
entries.what: Teshigahara's adaptation of Abe's novel: an entomologist is trapped in a sand pit with a woman who must shovel it out nightly to keep the village above from being buried
entries.why: Shares the proposition that daily labour, filmed closely enough and for long enough, becomes unbearable, and shares Haneke's attention to matter, with skin, grit and water held in extreme close-up. Against it: this is an allegory with a Takemitsu score, an erotic centre, and a protagonist who finally chooses his pit, which makes it a parable about acceptance. The Seventh Continent is a flat account of one Austrian family's actual bank account and offers no parable whatever.

entries.title: Werckmeister Harmonies
entries.what: Bela Tarr's black-and-white film in thirty-nine shots: a whale and a mob arrive on a lorry in a Hungarian town, and the town comes apart
entries.why: Tone is the match, the same grey exhaustion and the same sense of a society that has already ended and is waiting to be told so. Form is not, and the key has made this judgement once already in placing The Turin Horse at grade 1: Tarr's unbroken drifting long takes are the opposite of Haneke's method of cutting a life into discrete blocks separated by black leader. Werckmeister is further off again for being an allegory, with a mob, a whale and a prince in it. A rewarding pairing for a viewer, a weaker claim about the film.

entries.title: The Piano
entries.what: Jane Campion's film: a mute Scotswoman is shipped to colonial New Zealand with her daughter and her piano, and bargains the instrument back one key at a time
entries.why: The only link is a pun. Ada does not speak, and the target is routinely called silent — but Haneke's film is full of dialogue, it is simply dialogue that explains nothing. Campion's is an expressive romantic melodrama in which a Michael Nyman score does the heroine's feeling for her, which is the single technique Haneke most systematically denies himself: there is no music at all in The Seventh Continent apart from a car radio and the car wash. Opposite procedures on unrelated subjects.

entries.title: The Double Life of Veronique
entries.what: Krzysztof Kieślowski's film: two identical women, one in Kraków and one in Paris, who have never met and feel each other's lives
entries.why: 'Dreamlike, melancholic, existential musings' is the reason given, and Haneke's film is not dreamlike, not melancholic, and does not muse. It is a flat inventory of three years of a family's transactions, shot mostly in close-up on hands, taps and banknotes, ending in the methodical destruction of a household. Kieślowski's is lyrical, amber, scored throughout by Preisner and openly metaphysical. It already sits in the Avalon key, where the palette and the unverifiable second self do real work.

entries.title: The Secret in Their Eyes
entries.what: Juan José Campanella's Argentine film: a retired judicial investigator writes a novel about the 1974 case he never closed
entries.why: Warm, plot-driven, romantic and fully resolved, with a celebrated virtuoso crane shot into a football stadium — a film that means to move you and knows exactly how. Haneke's method is to withhold every device that would let you feel anything on the film's terms, including the reverse shot. 'Slow-burn, psychological, quiet despair' attaches to nothing in either picture.

entries.title: The Lighthouse
entries.what: Robert Eggers's black-and-white two-hander about two lighthouse keepers deteriorating on a New England rock
entries.why: The third target in this pool to receive this title. Nothing survives inspection: the Schober family are not isolated, they are embedded in a functioning Austrian society whose routines they perform impeccably right up until they stop, and that embedding is the entire point of the film. Eggers's is a study of two men escalating in confinement, with period profanity and enormous performances. 'Isolation, psychological unraveling, muted tones' fits several hundred films and this target is not one of them.

entries.title: The Wind Will Carry Us
entries.what: Abbas Kiarostami's film: a man from Tehran waits in a Kurdish village for an old woman to die so that he can film the funeral rite, and never explains to anyone, including the audience, what he is doing there
entries.why: Defensible on withholding, which is a real formal kinship: Kiarostami refuses to show his protagonist's colleagues, refuses to state his purpose, and lets the significant event happen off-screen — the same refusal Haneke makes about motive. But the key already holds the right Kiarostami. Taste of Cherry is about a man arranging his own death and treats it as a series of practical conversations, which is nearer in both subject and method. And The Wind Will Carry Us is sunlit, funny and finally generous about being alive, where The Seventh Continent is none of the three.

entries.title: The Tree of Life
entries.what: Terrence Malick's film: a Texas childhood in the 1950s set against the formation of the universe, narrated in whispered prayer
entries.why: The exact inverse of the target on every axis that matters. Malick supplies continuous interiority through voice-over, reaches for cosmic significance, and scores the film to Smetana, Tavener and Preisner; Haneke supplies no interiority at all, insists his family's act means nothing that can be stated, and uses no music. Both are slow, and that is the only true thing in 'poetic, contemplative, cosmic melancholy'.

entries.title: The Assassination of Jesse James
entries.what: Andrew Dominik's film, indexed in full as The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford: the last months of Jesse James and the courtship and murder committed by the man who idolised him, shot by Roger Deakins with period lens distortion
entries.why: Suggested for 'slow, meditative, tragic beauty', three qualities Haneke would regard as failures. The film is lyrical, heavily narrated, ravishingly photographed and openly elegiac about its subject; The Seventh Continent is deliberately ugly, refuses narration entirely, and denies its family any tragic stature whatever — it will not even let them be interesting. A famous slow film offered to a slow film.

entries.title: The Lobster
entries.what: Yorgos Lanthimos's film: single people are given forty-five days at a hotel to pair off or be converted into an animal of their choosing
entries.why: Real but second-best. Both films watch people perform the rituals of a bourgeois arrangement without believing in them, in flat frontal compositions, with an affect so level that cruelty arrives as administration. The key already holds Dogtooth at grade 2 for precisely this, and Dogtooth is the closer Lanthimos: a family sealed inside a house of its own rules, destroying itself from within, which is the target's situation exactly. The Lobster is an allegory with jokes and a voice-over narrator, and it explains its own rules at length, which Haneke never does about anything.

entries.title: The Red Turtle
entries.what: Michael Dudok de Wit's wordless animated feature: a castaway's raft is repeatedly destroyed by a turtle which then becomes a woman, and he lives out a life on the island
entries.why: 'Minimalist, poetic, human isolation', and the target is about none of these. The Schober family are not isolated and their problem is not solitude; they are employed, insured, socially intact and at the supermarket, and the horror of the film is that this turns out to be sufficient cause. The Red Turtle is a hand-drawn myth about accepting the life one is given, which is the consoling proposition Haneke's entire career exists to refuse.

entries.title: The Death of Mr. Lazarescu
entries.what: Cristi Puiu's film: an ailing old man in Bucharest calls an ambulance and is moved between four hospitals across one night — examined, lectured, deferred, transferred, and finally shaved for surgery he will not survive
entries.why: The closest thing in this pool to Haneke's discipline. A death is rendered as an accumulation of small administrative facts — forms, corridors, handovers, a nurse's patience running out — with no score, no reaction shots sold to the audience, and no moment at which the film indicates how to feel. It sits with the key's 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days as Romanian New Wave procedure, and arguably above it here, because its subject is a body processed by institutions that are not cruel, merely busy. Puiu's camera is handheld and his film is almost entirely talk, where Haneke nails the frame down and cuts to black leader; the coldness matches, the form does not.

entries.title: Home
entries.what: Ursula Meier's Swiss-French debut with Isabelle Huppert and Olivier Gourmet: a family living beside a disused motorway treat it as their garden, and when it finally opens to traffic they seal the house, brick up the windows and come apart inside it. Not the 2009 Arthus-Bertrand documentary or the 2015 DreamWorks film of the same name
entries.why: The best new pick for this target and close to essential. Meier's family answer an intrusion they cannot argue with by methodically converting their own home into the instrument of their destruction — insulating, then bricking, then breathing their own air — which is the Schober family's gesture of dismantling everything they own, performed as a sequence of household chores. Both films are built out of objects and routines shot close, both keep a refusing distance from the family's reasoning, and both end with the household abolished. Huppert connects it to the key's Piano Teacher besides. Meier does give her family a stated cause where Haneke gives none, and her last act tips toward the dreamlike; the surfaces, the register and the domestic horror match squarely.

entries.title: The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser
entries.aka: Every Man for Himself and God Against All
entries.what: Werner Herzog's German film, released as Jeder für sich und Gott gegen alle, with the non-professional Bruno S.: a man kept seventeen years in a cellar is set loose in 1828 Nuremberg, taught language and manners, and dies without ever being accounted for
entries.why: Herzog ends on Haneke's gesture. The autopsy turns up an enlarged liver and cerebellum, the officials are delighted to have something that will make a tidy report, and the film closes on that satisfaction — an explanation produced where none is possible, which is the same joke Haneke tells by refusing to supply one at all. New German Cinema is also the tradition Haneke arrives out of. Against it: the milieu is a parable of 1828, and the sensibility is warm, wry and openly lyrical, with Pachelbel's Canon, Albinoni's Adagio and dreamed Berbers in the Sahara — every consolation Haneke systematically denies himself. The key already holds the stronger version of this link at grade 3 in Fassbinder's Why Does Herr R. Run Amok?, where a man of the same class in the same national cinema annihilates his own family. Tone 1: austere and uningratiating, but it means to move you, and the target does not.

entries.title: Visitor Q
entries.what: Takashi Miike's digital-video feature, the last of the six straight-to-video Love Cinema films: a stranger moves in with a household whose father films everything, whose mother sells sex and takes heroin, and whose son beats her, and the family is restored by a killing they commit together
entries.why: The connection runs through the phrase family disintegration and nothing at all survives contact with either film. Miike's family is a cartoon of transgression built to be laughed at — incest, necrophilia and lactation played as gags on a camcorder — and the arc is redemptive: the household is repaired by the end. Haneke's Schobers are not dysfunctional in any sense a screenwriter could use. They are employed, insured, punctual and polite, nobody is visibly unhappy, and the horror of the film is precisely that this turns out to be sufficient cause; what they do is irreversible and is filmed as housework. Opposite subject, opposite volume, opposite conclusion. The camcorder is the only shared object in the two pictures, and the key already holds Benny's Video at grade 3 for what Haneke does with one.

entries.title: Happiness
entries.what: Todd Solondz's American black comedy: three New Jersey sisters, an obscene caller, and a suburban psychiatrist who drugs and rapes his son's schoolfriends, all played flat and set to a chipper title song
entries.why: The overlap is real and it is narrow. Both films hold a level, unjudging camera on the middle-class household and decline to supply the condemnation the material seems to be asking for. It stops there. Solondz is a comedian: the picture runs on punchlines, characterises everyone vividly, hands them confessional monologues, carries Robbie Kondor's score throughout and goes out on a joke. The Seventh Continent's whole method is to deny its family any interiority at all — no backstory, no stated motive, and the nearest thing to a confession is a dictated letter to the grandparents written in the language of a circular. The key keeps American Beauty at grade 1 for making this same insufficient claim; Happiness is the better film doing it. Tone 0: it is loud with laughter, and there are no jokes anywhere in Haneke's film.

entries.title: Stalker
entries.what: Andrei Tarkovsky's Soviet film from the Strugatsky brothers: a guide leads a writer and a scientist through a forbidden Zone toward a room said to grant your deepest wish, and at the door none of them will go in
entries.why: The ground is real and thin, and it is exactly the ground on which the key already holds Tarkovsky's Mirror at grade 1 with tone 0 — Tarkovsky is one of the eight directors on Haneke's 2012 Sight and Sound ballot. Beyond the name there is one rhyme worth stating: both films are about people who have staked everything on an elsewhere, the Room and Australia, that is never shown to work. But Tarkovsky arrives there via three men arguing about faith for two and a half hours over Artemyev's score and a camera that will not stop drifting, and Haneke arrives there in ninety minutes of nailed-down frames and banknotes going down a toilet. Grade and tone come apart as far as they do anywhere in this key: essential to know that Haneke admires Tarkovsky, useless as a guide to what watching Haneke is like.

entries.title: Ida
entries.what: Paweł Pawlikowski's Polish film, eighty-two minutes in Academy-ratio black and white shot by Łukasz Żal and Ryszard Lenczewski: a novice about to take her vows is sent to meet the aunt she did not know she had, a former Stalinist prosecutor, and learns that her parents were murdered Jews
entries.why: One scene is a direct match and it is worth the entry on its own. Wanda crosses to the window of her flat and is gone before the shot has finished — no score, no build, no reaction shot, no explanation offered afterwards. That is Haneke's handling of exactly the moment every other film underlines. Pawlikowski carries no extradiegetic music at all until a single Bach cue at the close, keeps the camera still, and leaves motive unspoken throughout. What keeps the grade at 1 is the subject: the target is about a healthy family's routine turning into its own abolition, with no history behind it and no cause anyone can name, while Ida's death has a war behind it, a named guilt and a stated reason, and the film around it is a period road picture with a jazz saxophonist and a love scene. Tone 1 rather than 2 because the rigour matches and the surfaces do not — Żal and Lenczewski's frames are beautiful, and The Seventh Continent's are deliberately, consumer-catalogue ugly.

entries.title: Clean, Shaven
entries.what: Lodge Kerrigan's American debut, seventy-nine minutes, with Peter Greene: a schizophrenic man newly out of an institution drives north to find the daughter who was adopted away, while a detective assembles a child-murder case around him
entries.why: Both are short, plotless by design, punishing to sit through, and refuse the explanation their subject seems to demand — Kerrigan gives no psychiatric account of Peter Winter any more than Haneke gives a motive for the Schobers, and both make you watch a body being worked on in unbroken close-up rather than cutting away, the fingernail and the scalp here, the fish on the carpet and the pills there. The inversion is the whole distance between them, though, and it is the method rather than the subject: Kerrigan's sound design — overlapping radio, scraping, static held at hostile volume — exists to put you inside the head, which is the one place Haneke will not take you. The Seventh Continent stays outside, at waist height, on the objects, and its most frightening property is quiet. Tone 1 for the shared austerity and the shared refusal, not 2, because one film assaults and the other withholds.

entries.title: Shame
entries.what: Steve McQueen's second feature, with Michael Fassbender and Carey Mulligan: a New York executive whose life is organised entirely around compulsive sex has the arrangement disturbed when his sister moves into his apartment
entries.why: The same director as the key's Hunger, working the same surface on material a good deal closer to this target. Almost the whole of Shame is a solvent professional's routine filmed as procedure inside a designed consumer interior — the laptop, the shower, the run, the transaction, the commute — held in long takes at a fixed distance with the interior life withheld, and the single line offered as an account of the man refuses to say what it is an account of. The suicide attempt is handled Haneke's way round: the act is off screen and what is on screen is the blood, the bathroom and the clearing up. It sits with the key's Time Out, the other film about a middle-class man dismantling his own life by increments while the routine holds. Grade and tone come apart exactly where Le Feu follet's do. Harry Escott's score, Sean Bobbitt's beautiful Manhattan and Fassbender weeping in the rain are an apparatus for delivering a man's anguish to you, and the target's whole method is to switch every one of those off and leave you outside at waist height, looking at the objects.

entries.title: Beau Travail
entries.what: Claire Denis's French film, loosely after Melville's Billy Budd: a Foreign Legion sergeant in Djibouti recalls from Marseille how he destroyed a recruit he envied, told largely through the unit's drills, laundry and ironing, and ending with him alone on a nightclub floor
entries.why: Real on form and thin on everything else. Denis builds the film almost entirely out of repeated ritual with the narrative connective tissue cut away, and she withholds Galoup's reasons as completely as Haneke withholds the Schobers' — the voice-over circles the question for ninety minutes and never arrives at a cause. That is the same bargain, and the key already rewards it in The Turin Horse and Marseille. But the ritual is filmed for the opposite effect. Agnes Godard's camera makes the exercises beautiful: they are choreographed, sunlit, salt-covered, and carried end to end by Britten's Billy Budd, which is an authored and exalting surface. Haneke films routine as tedium in consumer-catalogue ugliness with no music at all, and his subject is an affluent Austrian household abolishing itself, which has nothing whatever to do with a legionnaire's jealousy. The last dance is the proof of the distance: Denis ends on release, and The Seventh Continent ends on a television left running in an emptied flat.

entries.title: Killer of Sheep
entries.what: Charles Burnett's black-and-white first feature, shot at weekends in Watts across 1972 and 1973 for under ten thousand dollars as his UCLA thesis and first shown at the Whitney in 1978: Stan, a slaughterhouse worker too tired to feel anything, his family and his street, in loosely connected scenes with no plot
entries.why: The form is a genuine match and the argument is not. Burnett assembles the film out of discrete undramatised episodes with the connective tissue removed, refuses a crisis, refuses a resolution, and lets daily labour run at its own length until the labour is the content, which is what the key holds Jeanne Dielman and 71 Fragments for. Two things stop it there, and the second is decisive. Burnett loves these people and shows them to you — the children playing, the jokes, the marriage, faces held with open affection — where Haneke denies his family any interiority at all. And twenty-two records, Dinah Washington and Robeson and Armstrong and Earth, Wind and Fire, do the lifting and the consoling throughout, and there is no music in The Seventh Continent apart from a car radio and the car wash. The subject is inverted besides: Stan's problem is that he has neither money nor rest, and the horror of Haneke's film is that the Schobers have both and it turns out to be sufficient cause.

entries.title: Police, Adjective
entries.what: Corneliu Porumboiu's Romanian film: a detective in Vaslui spends days tailing a schoolboy who shares hashish with two friends, decides he will not make the arrest, and is answered by his captain, who sits him down with a dictionary and has him read out the definitions of conscience, law, moral and police
entries.why: Tone runs well ahead of grade, which is the pattern the key already uses for Marseille, Vive L'Amour and Our Daily Bread. There is no family here, no death and no consumer household, so the subject connection is remote. The method is not remote at all: frames nailed down and held for whole minutes on a man standing in a street waiting for nothing, no non-diegetic music anywhere in the film, flat unemphatic performance, and Cristi's typed surveillance reports put on screen in full so that the audience has to sit and read the paperwork, which is Haneke's attention to documents and surfaces exactly. One rhyme is worth the entry on its own: both films finish by handing you an official text instead of an ending. Porumboiu closes on definitions read aloud and a diagram chalked on a board, an authority manufacturing meaning out of language because none is otherwise available; Haneke closes on a flat factual card, a document standing where an explanation should be. The only deduction on tone is that Porumboiu is dryly funny and Haneke is not funny at all, and even that is delivered cold, withheld, and at the same level as everything else in the film.
